title: The wall at Sirhind
hookLine: the younger sons Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh, nine and six, are executed for refusing to convert; their grandmother Mata Gujri dies too

lines: A GRANDMOTHER AND TWO SMALL BOYS.
THE HARDEST STORY IN THE CAMP.
cards: On the riverbank, Mata Gujri, the Guru's mother, now an old woman, went one way with her two youngest grandsons, Zorawar Singh, about nine, and Fateh Singh, about six. A family servant offered to hide them in his village.
Tradition says he betrayed them for a reward, and they were handed over to the governor of Sirhind, Wazir Khan. It was the middle of winter. This is the hardest story in the camp.
Sikhs tell it to their children every December, very gently, and it's told gently here too.

teach.b: Sahibzade, a word Sikhs say with enormous love. It means sons of the master, and Sikhs use it for all four of the Guru's sons.
Tradition says the grandmother and the boys were kept in a cold tower open to the December wind, the Thanda Burj.
Each day the boys were brought before the governor's court and told: accept Islam, and you'll have everything; refuse, and you'll die.
Tradition says their grandmother told them stories of their grandfather and great-great-grandfather, the Gurus who gave their lives, and each day the boys walked in and refused.
They greeted the court, tradition says, with the Khalsa's own greeting, not a bow. Then someone in that court did something Sikhs have never forgotten.
The Nawab of Malerkotla, Sher Muhammad Khan, a Muslim nobleman whose own brother, tradition says, had died fighting the Guru, stood up and protested.
You cannot punish children for their father, he said; it is against justice and against Islam itself. He was overruled. Tradition says the boys were bricked into a wall, and then put to death.

teach.h: MATA GUJRI, AND TODAR MAL'S GOLD.
teach.b: When Mata Gujri heard, she died in the tower. A merchant named Todar Mal, tradition says, paid for land to cremate the three by covering it with gold coins.
Sikhs still honor the town of Malerkotla for the Nawab's protest, and Gurdwara Fatehgarh Sahib stands at Sirhind. Two boys, nine and six, who would not give up who they were.
That is why Sikhs say: the youngest were the bravest.

how: Each December, Sikhs remember the Sahibzade and Mata Gujri during Shaheedi Jor Mela at Fatehgarh Sahib, and many families hold simple gatherings, recitation and langar during that week.

games.why: Sher Muhammad Khan protested that punishing children was against justice and against Islam. Sikhs still honor Malerkotla for it.

practice: Hold one minute of silence, and say the names once, softly: Zorawar Singh, Fateh Singh, Mata Gujri. Then stay in the silence; no words are needed. If you pray, you can pray; if you don't, the silence is its own respect.

wordCard.voice: Sahibzade. The sons of the master, the Guru's four sons; the two youngest, nine and six, died at Sirhind rather than give up their faith.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi, from Persian: sons of the master, the Guru's four sons.

carryVoice: Your line: the youngest were the bravest. Sikhs carry these names through every December. That's day ninety.
